steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computer vision paper on DepthG, an unsupervised semantic segmentation method that uses depth to guide feature correlation and sampling. Motivate unsupervised segmentation, discuss STEGO and its follow-up, and explain our two ideas.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Semantic segmentation: applications and the cost of annotation
- Unsupervised semantic segmentation: STEGO and hidden positives
- Missing spatial information; using depth from a monocular estimator
- DepthG part 1: depth-feature correlations
- DepthG part 2: farthest-point sampling on depth; results and design benefits

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Semantic segmentation
  - critical in many vision systems: autonomous driving (cite), medical (cite), many more (cite)
  - until recently mostly supervised; large amounts of pixel-level annotations
  - sourcing images labor intensive; annotating large datasets costly
  - MS COCO (cite): more than 28K hours for around 164K images; Cityscapes (cite): 1.5 hours per image on average
- Unsupervised semantic segmentation
  - triggered by these costs; remove need for labeled data (cite)
  - Hamilton et al. (cite) accelerated progress; STEGO: DINO-pretrained (cite) ViT (cite) features, distilled across dataset, contrastive learning
  - features sampled randomly from same image, k-NN matched images, other negative images
  - Seong et al. (cite): hidden positives; exposes inefficiency of random sampling in STEGO, big improvements
  - both only pixel space, ignore spatial layout
- Depth
  - humans perceive in 3D; supervised segmentation benefits from spatial info in training (cite)
  - idea: depth maps into STEGO training; depth = product of vision, not a labeled signal
  - off-the-shelf zero-shot monocular depth estimator for benchmark datasets -> no human annotation or sensor ground truth
- DepthG (1)
  - guide model to learn rough spatial layout; hypothesis: helps differentiate objects
  - extend contrastive process to spatial dimension: Feature-Feature Correlations + Depth-Feature Correlations
  - pull apart features far apart in 3D, map closer if low distance in depth space; Figure 1
- DepthG (2)
  - Farthest-Point Sampling (FPS) (cite) on depth map, samples scenes equally in 3D
  - combined: SOTA across multiple benchmark datasets; short video in supplementary
  - first to bring 3D scene knowledge into unsupervised learning for 2D images without depth as network input
  - avoids input dependency -> no depth needed at inference, not affected by its availability/quality

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation has a critical role in many vision systems today, in a lot of domains. These include for example autonomous driving, medical applications, and many more. Until recently most of the research in this area focused on supervised models, which need a large amount of pixel-level annotations for training. Getting this image data is often labor intensive, and on top of that annotating the large datasets that are needed for good performance is very expensive. Several benchmark datasets report how long annotation took. For example, the MS COCO dataset needed more than 28K hours of human annotation for around 164K images, and annotating one image in the Cityscapes dataset took 1.5 hours on average. These costs led to unsupervised semantic segmentation, which tries to remove the need for labeled training data to train segmentation models. Recently the work by Hamilton et al. sped up the progress towards getting good results on semantic segmentation tasks without labels. Their model, STEGO, uses a DINO-pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract features, and these features are then distilled across the whole dataset with a contrastive learning approach to learn semantically relevant features. The features to be distilled are sampled randomly from feature maps of the same image, of k-NN matched images, and of other negative images. Seong et al. build on this by trying to find the features that are most relevant to the model by discovering hidden positives. Their work shows that random sampling in STEGO is inefficient, since hidden positives sampling gives significant improvements. But both approaches only work on the pixel space, so they do not take the spatial layout of the scene into account. We humans perceive the world in 3D, and also previous work has shown that supervised semantic segmentation can benefit a lot from spatial information during training. Because of this, we propose to add spatial information in the form of depth maps to the STEGO training process. Depth is seen as a product of vision and is not a labeled training signal. To get depth information for the benchmark image datasets we evaluate on, we use an off-the-shelf zero-shot monocular depth estimator that gives us spatial information about the scene. So we can use the depth information without needing human annotations or sensor ground truth.

- DepthG (1)
  - guide model to learn rough spatial layout of the scene; hypothesis: helps differentiate objects
  - extend contrastive process to the spatial dimension: not only Feature-Feature Correlations but also Depth-Feature Correlations
  - pull apart features with high distances in 3D, map closer if distance low in depth space; Figure 1
- DepthG (2)
  - Farthest-Point Sampling (FPS) on depth map -> samples scenes equally in 3D
  - together: SOTA in evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets; short video in supplementary
  - first to bring 3D scene knowledge into unsupervised learning for 2D images without depth maps as network input
  - no input dependency -> no depth at inference, unaffected by availability/quality of depth

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation has a critical role in many vision systems today, in a lot of domains. These include for example autonomous driving, medical applications, and many more. Until recently most of the research in this area focused on supervised models, which need a large amount of pixel-level annotations for training. Getting this image data is often labor intensive, and on top of that annotating the large datasets that are needed for good performance is very expensive. Several benchmark datasets report how long annotation took. For example, the MS COCO dataset needed more than 28K hours of human annotation for around 164K images, and annotating one image in the Cityscapes dataset took 1.5 hours on average. These costs led to unsupervised semantic segmentation, which tries to remove the need for labeled training data to train segmentation models. Recently the work by Hamilton et al. sped up the progress towards getting good results on semantic segmentation tasks without labels. Their model, STEGO, uses a DINO-pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract features, and these features are then distilled across the whole dataset with a contrastive learning approach to learn semantically relevant features. The features to be distilled are sampled randomly from feature maps of the same image, of k-NN matched images, and of other negative images. Seong et al. build on this by trying to find the features that are most relevant to the model by discovering hidden positives. Their work shows that random sampling in STEGO is inefficient, since hidden positives sampling gives significant improvements. But both approaches only work on the pixel space, so they do not take the spatial layout of the scene into account. We humans perceive the world in 3D, and also previous work has shown that supervised semantic segmentation can benefit a lot from spatial information during training. Because of this, we propose to add spatial information in the form of depth maps to the STEGO training process. Depth is seen as a product of vision and is not a labeled training signal. To get depth information for the benchmark image datasets we evaluate on, we use an off-the-shelf zero-shot monocular depth estimator that gives us spatial information about the scene. So we can use the depth information without needing human annotations or sensor ground truth.

With our method, DepthG, we first propose to (1) guide the model to learn a rough spatial layout of the scene, because we hypothesize that this will help the network to differentiate objects much better. We do this by extending the contrastive process to the spatial dimension, so the model does not only learn Feature-Feature Correlations, but also Depth-Feature Correlations. This way the model is guided to pull apart features that have high distances in 3D space, and to map them closer together if their distance in depth space is low. Figure 1 shows this process.

Since we now have information about the spatial layout of the scene, we also propose to (2) inform our feature sampling process spatially by using Farthest-Point Sampling (FPS) on the depth map, which samples scenes equally in 3D. We show that these techniques together make our approach to unsupervised segmentation very effective, because in our evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets we show state-of-the-art performance. A short video presenting our method is included in the supplementary materials. As far as we know, we are the first to propose a mechanism that brings 3D knowledge of the scene into unsupervised learning for 2D images without encoding depth maps as part of the network input. This part of the design reduces the risk that the model develops an input dependency. So our approach does not need depth information during inference and is not affected by whether such depth information is available or how good it is.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation plays a critical role in many of today’s vision systems in a multitude of domains. These include, among others, autonomous driving [1], medical applications [2,3], and many more [4,5,6,7]. Until recently, most research in this area focused on supervised models that require a large amount of pixel-level annotations for training. Not only is sourcing this image data often labor intensive, but annotating the large datasets required for good performance also comes at a high price. Several benchmark datasets report their annotation times. For example, the MS COCO dataset [8] required more than 28K hours of human annotation for around 164K images, and annotating a single image in the Cityscapes dataset [9] took 1.5 hours on average. These costs have led to the advent of unsupervised semantic segmentation [10,11,12,13], which aims to remove the need for labeled training data to train segmentation models. Recently, work by Hamilton et al. [12] has accelerated progress towards achieving good results on semantic segmentation tasks without labels. Their model, STEGO, uses a DINO-pretrained [14] Vision Transformer (ViT) [15] to extract features that are then distilled across the entire dataset to learn semantically relevant features, using a contrastive learning approach. The features to be distilled are sampled randomly from feature maps produced from the same image, k-NN matched images, and other negative images. Seong et al. [13] build on this process by trying to identify the features most relevant to the model by discovering hidden positives. Their work exposes an inefficiency of random sampling in STEGO, as hidden positives sampling leads to significant improvements. However, both approaches only operate on the pixel space and therefore fail to take the spatial layout of the scene into account. Not only do we humans perceive the world in 3D, but previous work [16,17,18,19,20,21] has also shown that supervised semantic segmentation can benefit greatly from spatial information during training. Inspired by these observations, we propose to incorporate spatial information in the form of depth maps into the STEGO training process. Depth is considered a product of vision and does not provide a labeled training signal. To obtain depth information for the benchmark image datasets in our evaluations, we use an off-the-shelf zero-shot monocular depth estimator to get spatial information about the scene. This allows us to incorporate depth information without the need for human annotations or sensor ground truth.

With our method, DepthG, we propose to (1) guide the model to learn a rough spatial layout of the scene, since we hypothesize this will help the network differentiate objects much better. We achieve this by extending the contrastive process to the spatial dimension: we do not limit the model to learning only Feature-Feature Correlations, but also Depth-Feature Correlations. Through this process, the model is guided towards pulling apart features with high distances in 3D space, and mapping them closer together if their distance in depth space is low. Figure 1 visualizes this process.

With information about the spatial layout of the scene available, we further propose to (2) spatially inform our feature sampling process by using Farthest-Point Sampling (FPS) [22,23] on the depth map, which samples scenes equally in 3D. We show that these techniques in combination make our approach to unsupervised segmentation highly effective, as our evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. We include a short video presenting our method in the supplementary materials. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a mechanism to incorporate 3D knowledge of the scene into unsupervised learning for 2D images without encoding depth maps as part of the network input. This design aspect alleviates the risk of the model developing an input dependency. Therefore, our approach does not rely on depth information during inference and is not affected by the availability or quality of such depth information.
